title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 6: A Revitalized Legal Profession
primary_topics: Chapter 6 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- CJP's testimonial-dinner address to the assembled Philippine bar associations, setting out his twin visions of a reformed judiciary and a revitalized legal profession as the means to safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity.

His standard for lawyers: competence coupled with ethics, an ethical compass that places truth and justice above the lawyer's own and the client's interests, against the drift toward lawyers as mere technicians of the law.

An enlistment of the bar in the fight against the four ACID problems -- limited access to justice by the poor, corruption, incompetence and delay -- on the argument that the judiciary alone can win only half the battle.

The concrete reform projects he offers as the profession's points of entry: pro bono incentives, the e-payment system, a stricter nomination process, halls of justice, and computerization of the courts.
sub_topics: His thanks to the twelve bar and legal organizations jointly hosting the testimonial dinner, from the IBP and PBA to MARLAW, PDRCI, PICA, the UIA and WILOCI, noting how rarely they come together under one roof.

The Proclamation No. 1017 petitions in which IBP President Jose Anselmo Cadiz and other IBP officers were petitioners, and the nine-hour Oral Argument of March 7, 2006 that ran to 10:00 p.m. in a jam-packed session hall.

His confidentiality rule preventing comment on the case internals, and his use of it only to underscore the bar's role, including IBP activity in the Executive Order No. 464 and 'state of rebellion' or Oakwood mutiny cases.

The twin visions restated: a judiciary of four Ins, morally courageous against influence, interference, indifference and insolence, and impervious to the plague of 'ships'; and a revitalized bar that is responsible, dependable and morally upright.
His pledge to continue CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr.'s judicial reform program but, given a time-limited incumbency, to focus on the four ACID problems.

The constitutional grounding of Liberty and Prosperity: the Bill of Rights for liberty, and the Declaration of Principles and Article XII's mandate of a 'more equitable distribution of opportunities, income and wealth' for prosperity as an economic right.
Lawyers' role in shaping public opinion and reflecting the nation's pulse, being consulted on presidential issuances, legislation, elections and even fashion.
His indictment of a hierarchy of responsibilities in which lawyers put their own interests first, the client's second and justice a far third.

Ethics as inseparable from competence: rules of professional conduct cannot define ethical conduct exhaustively, so an internalized ethical compass is required and quality justice begins with a high standard of ethics.

The five key areas of reform in which he seeks the profession's cooperation, enumerated from the January 12, 2006 strategic planning workshop: legal aid incentives, e-payment, a proactive nomination process with stricter discipline, halls of justice and court computerization with skills-based training.
The e-payment system launching April 21, under which docket and other fees go directly to the Land Bank of the Philippines rather than to clerks of court.

The complete computerization of the Sandiganbayan launched March 14, 2006, digitizing all pleadings and orders in its 2,700 pending cases, which with the e-library presages a paperless and more transparent judiciary.
His closing request for the bar's support in making the vision real, delivered with thanks in Filipino.

stances.claim: Competence in the law is not enough; it must be coupled with ethics, because rules of professional conduct can never enumerate the myriad situations of practice and so an internalized ethical compass is what actually governs a lawyer's conduct.
stances.rhetorical_move: limits-of-codification argument: the impossibility of exhaustive rules is turned into the case for internalized character

stances.claim: Many lawyers have inverted their hierarchy of responsibilities, putting their own interests first, their clients' second and justice a far third, having become technicians of the law who treat it as an end rather than a means.
stances.rhetorical_move: diagnosis-by-inversion: naming the correct order of duties and showing the profession has reversed it

stances.claim: The ACID problems cannot be solved by the judiciary alone; the battle would only be half won without the legal profession, so lawyers must take on legal aid, anti-corruption, nomination and anti-delay reforms as their own.
stances.rhetorical_move: shared-burden appeal followed by five concrete, already-funded projects the audience can join

stances.claim: The twin visions of a reformed judiciary and a revitalized legal profession are means to the loftier goals of safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity, which are restatements of democracy and development, ethics and economics, integrity and investments.
stances.rhetorical_move: means-and-ends framing with paired-antithesis restatement of the governing philosophy

IBP President Jose Anselmo Cadiz and other IBP officers appearing as petitioners against Proclamation No. 1017 and enduring a nine-hour Oral Argument on March 7, 2006 that ran until 10:00 p.m. in a jam-packed session hall.

The Sandiganbayan computerization he launched on March 14, 2006, with all pleadings, even motions for postponement, and all orders in its 2,700 pending cases already digitized and accessible.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' reproduced the address Chief Justice Panganiban delivered at a testimonial dinner jointly tendered by twelve Philippine bar and legal organizations, an occasion he noted was rare in bringing them all under one roof. He opened with the Proclamation No. 1017 petitions, in which IBP President Jose Anselmo Cadiz and other IBP officers were petitioners and had endured a nine-hour Oral Argument on March 7, 2006 that ran to 10:00 p.m.; invoking the Court's confidentiality rule, he declined to discuss the case and used it only to show how much the nation's destiny depends on how lawyers advocate public-interest causes, noting the IBP's activity as well in the Executive Order No. 464 and Oakwood mutiny cases. He restated the twin visions announced at the start of his chief justiceship: a judiciary of four Ins -- integrity, independence, industry and intelligence -- impervious to the plague of 'ships,' and a revitalized legal profession that is responsible, dependable and morally upright and whose members stand for their convictions against all odds. Both, he said, serve the loftier goals of safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity, grounded in the Bill of Rights and in Article XII's mandate of a more equitable distribution of opportunities, income and wealth. He criticized lawyers who had become technicians of the law, inverting their duties so that justice came a far third, and argued that because rules of conduct can never cover the myriad situations of practice, an internalized ethical compass is required, recalling how his firm had declined a sizeable retainer from a businessman who asked whether they knew the judge. He then enlisted the bar against the four ACID problems, since the battle would be only half won without them, listing reforms from the January 12, 2006 strategic planning workshop: pro bono incentives, the April 21 e-payment system through Land Bank, a stricter nomination process, more halls of justice, and computerization, exemplified by the Sandiganbayan's digitized 2,700 cases.
